new_statements.quote: The word in Itonama consists of two or more syllables. Its boundaries are marked by a complex of penultimate stress and plus juncture. [...] Any Itonama word (we use 'word' as a phonological term, equivalent to 'foot' or 'stress group' in other discussions; most phonological words are also grammatical words) consists of two to seven syllables, the next to last of which is stressed. [...] There are a few Spanish loans that have antepenultimate stress in the speech of some speakers of Itonama. For these speakers it would be necessary to recognize the stress peak of each word as phonemically relevant; however, for the most speakers the stress can simply be considered part of a complex word boundary signal.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the source the catalog record (our earlier survey-2026-08-31, penultimate stress, window 2-7) was built from; reading the full text confirms the quoted passage and the 2-7 syllable window. Quote is from the ABBYY scanned of the scan; stray scanned symbols (♦, ^, stray digits) were dropped and the text otherwise left as printed. Fieldwork base: Nueva Calama, Magdalena and Huacaraje.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every phonological word has two to seven syllables and is stressed on the penultimate syllable; stress plus juncture is the word-boundary signal and is not contrastive. Example given of the loan exception: es'piritu 'spirit' with antepenultimate stress. Superimposed on this is a three-level word intonation (pitch) system that is not lexical ('not innate to the word as a morphophonemic unit'); phonetic pitch 4 occurs only on stressed syllables, and no pitch rise from the stressed to the final syllable is ever observed.
new_statements.exceptions: A few Spanish loans carry antepenultimate stress for some speakers (es'piritu 'spirit'); for those speakers stress would have to be treated as phonemic, for most speakers it is predictable (part of the word-boundary complex).
new_statements.identity_note: Liccardi & Grimes recorded their data over fourteen months in Nueva Calama, Magdalena and Huacaraje (Iténez province). Camp & Liccardi's 1967 vocabulary introduction says the Itonama of San Ramón differs only in a few lexical items and in the ch/ts fluctuation from that of Magdalena and Huacaraje; no dialect difference in stress is reported anywhere. Crevels worked 2000-2006 with the last speakers in Magdalena.
